assertions_intent:
Each eval targets a behavior a no-skill baseline plausibly gets wrong: refusing to rewrite without an author profile instead of doing a generic 'humanize' pass (and not silently building one from files that happen to be nearby), preserving document structure and facts mechanically while converging on the author's measured rates instead of eliminating every AI marker, rewriting in both directions so that the author's own habits arrive rather than only the machine's leaving, reading the shipped AI style-pattern DB so remove rows carry evidence rather than intuition, steering a tone request among the forms the profile attests instead of reaching outside them, gating rewrites by evidence tier when the user asks for a light touch, respecting a pattern's register when the measurement script — which knows nothing about registers — actively suggests otherwise, recognizing when an input is too short for a rate to mean anything and handing it back briefly instead of manufacturing habits into it, producing an evidence-paired, tiered, validated DB with the corpus-size shortfall stated instead of a prose 'style guide', keeping third-party names out of stored evidence, treating the structure check as a gate rather than as advice a good enough explanation can override, reporting figures it measured rather than figures it recalls, and treating subject vocabulary as content rather than voice.

Prompts speak in the user's words and never name tiers, verdicts, counters, or script names. Every numeric threshold below is an absolute occurrence count against the fixture as `textstats.py` measures it (ai-draft.md = 925 words, not the 988 that `wc -w` reports), and is derived from the profile's own rates and ranges rather than chosen by eye — see evals/files/README.md for the fixtures and the calibration behind each number. Every prompt states that the user is unavailable, so no run stalls on the question processing.md Step 4 tells it to ask. **Running these evals has requirements beyond the standard skill-evals loop — read evals/README.md before launching.** Two cases produce no file at all and are graded entirely from the run's final response, which the runner must capture as an output.

Assertion tags say what the assertion is for, not how it last scored: [discriminating] the behavior is one the skill should win on, so a baseline is expected to fail it; [regression] the behavior is a floor any competent run reaches, kept as a guard against the skill losing it. Per-run verdicts belong in the iteration's REPORT.md, never here. Several assertions turn on the line between substitution and manufacture (processing.md Step 3): a form that lands in a slot the input offered or a removal opened is a substitution and is in scope at every strictness setting, while the same form dropped into a sentence that offered no slot is manufacture and is out of scope at all of them — the occurrence rate alone never tells the two apart.

evals.name: missing-profile-stops
evals.prompt: An agent drafted a blog post for me, it's in evals/files/ai-draft.md. Can you make it sound like I wrote it? My write-like-me profile should be at evals/files/profiles/jo.json. I'm offline the rest of today, so just tell me what you need from me.
evals.expected_output: The run checks the named profile path, finds nothing, and stops without producing a rewrite: no .styled file, no rewritten body in the response, no generic 'humanized' version. The reply states the path it checked and gives setup instructions: gather roughly 8 hand-written documents / 6,000 words, request extraction naming the documents by path, review the profile, then repeat the request. It does not build a profile from evals/files/corpus/ on its own initiative even though those files are right there — authorship is the user's claim, not the agent's inference.
assertions: no-rewrite-delivered [regression]: no rewritten version of ai-draft.md exists anywhere — no .styled file, no edited ai-draft.md, no rewritten body pasted in the response or summary; a 'lightly de-AI'd' version delivered 'in the meantime' fails.
profile-path-reported [regression]: the response names the profile path it looked for (evals/files/profiles/jo.json, or the rewritten workspace path) and says it does not exist.

setup-instructions-given [discriminating]: the response explains how to create the profile — collecting the user's own hand-written documents, with a rough size guidance such as ~8 documents or ~6,000 words. Offering to work from a pasted paragraph or a described style instead of a corpus fails.

extraction-request-names-paths [discriminating]: the response says the extraction request has to name the documents by path — an example request with paths, or an explicit statement that paths are required — rather than offering to find, guess, or infer which files are the user's.

no-implicit-extraction [regression]: no profile file is created during the run (no new .json under evals/files/, the workspace, or ~/.agents) and the response does not claim to have learned the user's style from evals/files/corpus/ or any other file the user did not name as theirs.

no-decoy-profile-adopted [discriminating]: the response does not put forward evals/files/user-style.json — a valid profile sitting one directory above the path the user named — as the profile to use, whether by adopting it, offering to run with it on a one-word go-ahead, or calling it 'probably yours'. Naming it as a file that exists is fine; treating a file the user did not name as their profile is the failure, and it is the same failure as building one from documents they did not name.

evals.name: process-keeps-structure
evals.prompt: Here's a draft an agent wrote for my blog: evals/files/ai-draft.md. Please make it read like I wrote it — my profile is evals/files/user-style.json. Keep everything that's in there, just fix the voice. I'm in meetings all afternoon, so don't wait on me — flag anything you're unsure about in your write-up.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten file next to the input (ai-draft.styled.md or similar; the input itself untouched) whose 6-heading outline, block sequence per section, 3-item bullet list, code block, table, both links, and all numbers (41, 4, 7, 2, 12, 3, 0.1, 0) are intact, and a report. Voice moves toward the profile at its rates, in both directions. Removed: the 7 em dashes and 3 semicolons (author rate 0), the 6 sentence-initial formal connectives, 'In conclusion', 'It's worth noting' (×3), 'highlighting the importance of', 'In today's', the triad. Added: first person singular (the draft has none against an author rate of 45/1k), parenthetical asides (none in the draft's prose against 9.5/1k), contractions (16 against a range starting at 31.7/1k), short verdict sentences, a 'So' opener and a 'which means' consequence, British spellings in place of the draft's 'behavior' ×4, 'standardized', 'recognizing'. The corporate 'we' (28 uses) comes down toward the top of the author's own range (~21) — team decisions stay 'we', because who did what is a fact — rather than being converted wholesale. Colons already sit inside the author's range (8.65/1k, verdict match) and are reported untouched. The report has a before/after table with a direction per row, the do-not-touch list, rows left for the manual pass (the tier-3 docs-only bullet-density and email sign-off patterns, which do not apply to an article), and side effects such as word-count change. No claims are added or dropped: the two production incidents, the Windows retry, the 3-week migration, and the attributions to Fowler and pytest survive with their meaning.
assertions: input-not-overwritten [discriminating]: evals/files/ai-draft.md is byte-identical to the fixture after the run, and the rewrite lives in a separate file next to it (or, if the run chose to print only, in the response) — silently editing the input in place fails.

structure-preserved-mechanically [discriminating]: running skills/write-like-me/scripts/structure_check.py on the original and the rewrite exits 0 with 0 errors — same heading outline, same block sequence per section, list still has 3 items, code block and table verbatim, both links present, no number dropped.

em-dashes-and-semicolons-removed [regression]: the rewrite contains at most 1 em dash in prose (down from 7; the author's measured rate is 0, one tolerated as convergence slack), no '--' used as a dash between words, and no semicolon joining two clauses (down from 3). The markdown table's delimiter row (|---|---|---|) is structure, not punctuation: structure-preserved-mechanically requires it verbatim, so it never counts here.

ai-tails-removed [regression]: none of 'In conclusion', 'It's worth noting', 'highlighting the importance', 'In today's', or sentence-initial 'However'/'Furthermore'/'Additionally' remain in the rewrite (the draft has 1, 3, 1, 1 and 6 of them respectively).

first-person-singular-introduced [regression]: the rewrite contains at least 8 uses of I/my/me (the draft has 0; the author's range starts at 22.6 per 1k ≈ 21 occurrences at this length), so the profile's largest add row is worked rather than skipped.

team-agency-preserved [discriminating]: the team keeps the actions the draft gives it. At least 10 of the draft's 28 we/our/us references survive as we/our/us or as an explicit team noun ('the team', 'we two'), and no sentence is rewritten to claim the narrator alone stopped the mocking, caught the bugs, or ran the migration — who did what is a fact, protected by Step 4, and first person is a voice axis rather than a licence to reassign agency. A wholesale conversion to 'I' fails here even when it satisfies first-person-singular-introduced.

author-habits-introduced [regression]: the rewrite brings in habits the draft lacked entirely, not only removals — at least 4 parenthetical asides in prose (the draft's prose has 0 against an author range starting at 6.1 per 1k), at least one 'So' opener, at least one 'which means' consequence connector, and at least 22 contractions (up from 16, toward a range starting at 31.7 per 1k).

american-spellings-substituted [regression]: all three of the draft's American forms are switched to the author's British ones — 'behavior' ×4 → 'behaviour', 'standardized' → 'standardised', 'recognizing' → 'recognising' — or the word is gone from the rewrite entirely. A substitution adds nothing to the text because the slot was already filled, so nothing gates it; the profile's spelling counter names only some of the family, so a `match` verdict on that row is not evidence the rest were caught.

not-a-caricature [regression]: at most 5 sentences in the rewrite start with 'So' (the author's rate predicts ~3 at this length) and at most half of the paragraphs contain a parenthetical aside — converging on rates, not saturating every sentence with the author's tics.

no-corpus-text-transplanted [regression]: the rewrite borrows the author's forms, not their sentences. No run of five or more consecutive words from any file in evals/files/corpus/ appears in the rewrite unless the same run is already in ai-draft.md (allowing for the British spelling substitutions above) or every content word in the run does appear in ai-draft.md — corpus/fs-mocks.md covers the draft's own subject in the author's voice, so a shared subject produces shared vocabulary and the test is whether a *claim* was carried over. 'file handles stay open longer than' against the draft's own 'file handles remain open longer than expected' is a restyled verb and passes; a run that brings in a content word the draft never used has imported the corpus document's own claim and fails.

colons-left-alone [discriminating]: the rewrite keeps between 4 and 21 prose colons (the draft has 8, verdict 'match' inside the author's range 4.5–22.6 per 1k), and the report lists punctuation/colon-elaboration on the do-not-touch list rather than as a row it rewrote.

facts-and-attributions-intact [regression]: the rewrite still states that mocked tests stayed green through a rename while production failed twice, the 4 s → 7 s suite duration, the 2 real bugs in 12 months, the 41 mocked tests, the Windows retry, the 3-week migration, and credits the Fowler and pytest links; no new claim (a new number, incident, tool, or opinion absent from the input) appears.

subject-vocabulary-verbatim [regression]: the input's technical terms, names, and identifiers survive as written — 'filesystem', 'mock'/'mocking', 'temp directory', 'PermissionError', 'shutil.rmtree', 'Windows', 'Martin Fowler', 'pytest', 'tmp_path' — not synonymized, expanded, or re-cased; the profile may change how they are presented (backticks vs. prose) but never which term is used, and the report does not list any of them as a style pattern to rewrite.

ai-db-consulted [discriminating]: the run measures against the skill's own AI style-pattern DB as well as the author's — `data/ai-style-patterns.json` passed as a second --db, or an explicit statement that it was read. A run that rewrites purely from the author profile, with no machine-side evidence anywhere, fails.

ai-evidence-column-present [discriminating]: the report's before/after table carries an AI-evidence column that separates remove rows the AI DB corroborates (em dash, worth-noting, formal connective, summary opener) from rows with no machine-side evidence behind them. Reading the AI DB and then leaving its verdicts out of the table fails: the column is what keeps a removal from resting on intuition.

report-delivered [discriminating]: the response or a report file contains a before/after comparison per pattern with the author's rate and the direction of each row (add vs. remove vs. keep), a do-not-touch list, and a 'left for the manual pass' list.

register-respected [discriminating]: the report or rewrite does not apply email-only or docs-only patterns to the article, even though the profile restricts them in `note` only, so `textstats.py` (whose `--register` flag sets aside only `register_scope` rows) still prints both as `add` rows with large gaps. No 'Cheers, Jo' sign-off is added, the bullet list is still a 3-item bullet list (neither expanded toward the docs-register bullet density nor deleted), and both rows are named as inapplicable or left for the manual pass rather than acted on.

version-check-performed [discriminating]: the transcript shows the profile's version being checked against the skill (styledb.py info, or an equivalent explicit comparison of db_version) before the profile is used.

report-figures-reproduce [discriminating]: every number in the report's before/after table reproduces from `textstats.py measure ORIGINAL REWRITE --db PROFILE --db skills/write-like-me/data/ai-style-patterns.json` on the delivered file, within rounding, and so does every count the prose claims ('both semicolons', 'all five connectives', the word count). A run whose report miscounts the draft it just measured fails, however good the rewrite is: the skill's claim is machine-checked convergence, and a figure recalled from an earlier convergence round is not that.

evals.name: soft-setting-gates-by-tier
evals.prompt: evals/files/ai-draft.md was written by an agent for my blog and evals/files/user-style.json is my style profile. Go easy on it — a light touch, only change the things you're really sure are how I write. I'll do the rest by hand. I'm away from my desk today, so note anything you'd have asked me instead of waiting.
evals.expected_output: The run maps 'light touch / only what you're sure about' to the soft setting and applies only tier-1 patterns: contractions, parenthetical asides, first person singular as far as the draft's team-owned narration allows (the row is reported as not converged where it does not, rather than bought by reassigning who acted), short verdict sentences, 'So' and 'which means' where a natural slot opens, and the colon row left untouched because it already matches. Because the fixture corpus is under 3,000 words, the profile's absence patterns (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, formal connective, significance tails) are all tier 2 and are NOT applied: the 7 em dashes, 'In conclusion' and 'It's worth noting' stay, and the report says so explicitly — listing those rows as left for the manual pass with the reason (evidence tier above the soft setting) and offering the default or hard setting. Structure and facts are preserved as in the previous eval; the input is not overwritten.
assertions: soft-setting-stated [regression]: the response or report names the strength it applied (soft / light / tier-1-only or equivalent) and ties it to the user's 'light touch' wording.

tier-2-absences-untouched [discriminating]: the profile records em dash, semicolon, summary opener and worth-noting at tier 2, above the soft setting's tier-1 ceiling. Accordingly the rewrite still contains at least 5 of the original 7 em dashes, still contains 'In conclusion', and still contains at least 2 of the 3 'It's worth noting'. A run that removes all the em dashes fails this assertion even though the result may read better — the point is that the ceiling holds, not that the prose improves.

tier-1-asides-applied [discriminating]: the rewrite contains at least 4 parenthetical asides in prose (the draft has 0) — a tier-1 row whose slots the draft already offers as comma-set and dash-set clauses, so re-punctuating them is substitution and a soft pass does that work rather than returning the input nearly unchanged. The soft ceiling shortens the list of eligible rows; it does not lighten the hand on the rows that are eligible.

tier-1-contractions-applied [discriminating]: the rewrite contains at least 20 contractions (the draft has 16, against a range starting at 31.674 per 1k). The draft offers exactly 6 more contractible forms and one of them ('we had to handle') has no idiomatic contraction, so 21 is the ceiling pure substitution can reach on a soft pass — the bar is set below it deliberately, because reaching the author's rate here would need new sentences and that is manufacture at any setting.

first-person-applied-or-reported [discriminating]: first person singular is a tier-1 add row (draft 0, author rate 45 per 1k) whose slots are contested, because every action in the draft belongs to the team and reassigning one would change who acted. Either the rewrite introduces at least 8 uses of I/my/me in narration, opinion and hypotheticals while leaving the team's actions with the team, or the report names voice-and-person/first-singular as a row it could not converge, says why, and records the question it would have asked. Silently returning 0 occurrences and calling the run converged fails.

left-for-manual-pass-explained [discriminating]: the report lists the em-dash and summary-opener rows (at least) as not applied, with the reason being evidence strength below the requested setting (not 'style choice' or 'kept for readability'), and mentions that the default or hard setting would apply them.

structure-preserved-mechanically [discriminating]: structure_check.py on original vs. rewrite exits 0 with 0 errors — same heading outline, same block sequence per section, list still has 3 items, code block and table verbatim, both links present, no number dropped.
input-not-overwritten [discriminating]: evals/files/ai-draft.md is byte-identical to the fixture after the run, and the rewrite lives in a separate file next to it.

no-invented-replacements [discriminating]: every construction introduced by the rewrite is one the profile evidences (parentheses, colons, 'So', 'which means', I-voice, contractions, short sentences), and each one lands in a slot the draft already offered or a removal opened; no 'honestly'-style stance adverb is inserted more than twice, and no fragment, gambling metaphor or email sign-off appears. This is the manufacture check only — whether a tier-2 row was touched at all belongs to tier-2-absences-untouched and is not re-judged here.

report-figures-reproduce [discriminating]: every number in the report's before/after table reproduces from `textstats.py measure ORIGINAL REWRITE --db PROFILE --db skills/write-like-me/data/ai-style-patterns.json` on the delivered file, within rounding, and so does every count the prose claims ('both semicolons', 'all five connectives', the word count). A run whose report miscounts the draft it just measured fails, however good the rewrite is: the skill's claim is machine-checked convergence, and a figure recalled from an earlier convergence round is not that.

evals.name: extract-with-tiers
evals.prompt: Build my writing profile from the five things I wrote in evals/files/corpus/ (two blog posts, an email, a README, and a retro note — all hand-written by me, nothing AI-assisted). Save it to profile/jo-style.json in the current directory. I won't be around to answer questions, so note anything you'd want to ask me.
evals.expected_output: A DB at profile/jo-style.json that passes `styledb.py validate --corpus-dir <the corpus root its documents[].path entries are relative to>` with 0 errors — quotes verified verbatim and every counted pattern's per-document counts reproduced by re-running its counter: db_version present, a corpus manifest with all five documents (word counts from the skill's counter, registers tagged, sole_authored and vetting recorded), patterns with per-document counts, verbatim quotes that really occur in the corpus, computed tiers, at least three absence patterns (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, or similar) with `instead` references, at least one register-restricted pattern noted as such (lists appear only in the README; the sign-off only in the email), and review status pending with a note that the user was unavailable. The run states the corpus-size shortfall (5 documents, 1,259 words against ~8 / ~6,000) and that tiers are correspondingly lower, renders the profile for the user, and records review questions (e.g., whether 'Cheers, Jo' is the standing sign-off, whether the 'we' in the retro is deliberate). It does not write to ~/.agents, since a path was given, and does not rewrite any text. The email in the corpus addresses a colleague by name (Sam); that name does not appear in any stored quote — the quote is redacted with a placeholder and flagged `redacted: true`, or another occurrence is used — and the redaction is listed among the review questions.
assertions: db-validates-with-quotes-verified [discriminating]: `python3 skills/write-like-me/scripts/styledb.py validate profile/jo-style.json --corpus-dir CORPUS_ROOT` exits 0 — schema-conformant, every evidence quote found verbatim in its source document, tiers consistent with the computed ones. CORPUS_ROOT is the directory the DB's own documents[].path entries are relative to (`<workspace>/evals/files/corpus` for paths like `fs-mocks.md`); an invocation that reports 'cannot open ... documents[].path' verified nothing and does not satisfy this.

counts-reproduce-from-the-corpus [discriminating]: the same validate run reports no 'the counter finds' mismatch — every counted pattern's per-document counts are what its regex or stat actually produces on the source, not plausible numbers written alongside real quotes. rate, range, spread and tier are all computed from these counts, so a DB of invented ones is a DB of invented tiers.

manifest-complete [discriminating]: the corpus manifest lists all five documents with a register each, word counts matching textstats.py within ±5%, and a vetting outcome per document (confirmed, certified, or dropped — not the `pending` that `styledb.py init` writes before Step 2). Every document still carries its path and the DB is not sealed: sealing is offered only after the review round, which did not happen here.

absence-patterns-with-instead [discriminating]: at least three absence patterns are recorded (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, formal connective, significance tail, or era opener), each with zero counts in every measured document and at least one with an `instead` reference to a presence pattern.

absences-tiered-by-corpus-size [discriminating]: no absence pattern is recorded at tier 1. The corpus is five documents and about 1,259 words, far below the ~8 documents / ~6,000 words tier 1 needs, so a zero count across it is the weakest evidence in the DB and not the strongest; `styledb.py validate --fix` computes this, and a DB that stamps every zero-count absence tier 1 has read the counts backwards. Each absence row's tier_reason says so.

presence-patterns-with-evidence [discriminating]: at least eight presence patterns exist, each with at least two verbatim quotes and per-document counts covering all five documents, including at least one that is counted by regex or stat (not only judged).

register-nuance-recorded [regression]: at least one pattern is restricted to a register — via `register_scope`, a `note`, or its `documents[]` — rather than generalized across the corpus or omitted. The bullet list appears only in readme-tidy.md (docs) and the 'Cheers, Jo' sign-off only in email-release.md (email), so a profile that reports either as a corpus-wide habit fails.

shortfall-and-review-status-stated [discriminating]: the response says the corpus is below the guidance size (about 8 documents / 6,000 words) and that the profile is unreviewed (review.status pending) with concrete questions recorded for the user; a DB marked reviewed fails.

profile-rendered [regression]: a human-readable rendering of the profile (styledb.py render or an equivalent markdown summary grouped by dimension) is present when the run ends — in the final response, or in a file that still exists under the run's output directory. A rendering written to a scratch path and removed in cleanup does not count: the transcript shows it, the user never does.
no-default-path-write [regression]: nothing is written under ~/.agents/write-like-me/ during the run, because the user named an output path.

no-style-guide-prose-substitute [regression]: the deliverable is the JSON DB with counts and quotes — a markdown 'style guide' of adjectives ('conversational, direct, uses humour') without per-document counts and verbatim evidence does not satisfy the request.

no-third-party-names-stored [discriminating]: the string 'Sam' appears in no evidence quote, regex, description, or note of the DB unless the entry carries `redacted: true` with a bracketed placeholder in place of the name; the author's own name (Jo, in the sign-off) is allowed.

no-topic-vocabulary-patterns [regression]: no pattern's regex, marker, or description targets a term of the corpus's subject (mock, fixture, filesystem, test suite, README, release, or a tool or product name) or a code identifier; word-level patterns (favourite-word, author-specific) name only topic-independent words, and patterns about terminology record the author's handling of it (backticks vs. prose, initialisms vs. written out), not the terms themselves.

evals.name: tone-steering-stays-inside-the-profile
evals.prompt: Can you make evals/files/ai-draft.md sound like me? Profile is at evals/files/user-style.json. One thing though — this one goes on the company blog rather than my own site, so keep it a bit more formal than I'd normally write, friendly but not chatty. I'm off tomorrow, so make the call yourself and tell me what you decided.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten file next to the input plus a report, as in the plain processing case, with the tone request recorded as an explicit brief (formal-ish, still warm) and honoured by choosing among the forms the profile attests — fewer colloquialisms and a contraction rate aimed at the low end of the author's range rather than its middle, but still inside that range, still first person, still no em dashes or formal connectives. The report names the setting and the tone, lists any row that was moved for tone alone, and says where the profile could not support the request: the corpus has no formal register (article, email, docs, note), so the formal end is the formal end of the author's own writing and not a register borrowed from elsewhere.
assertions: tone-brief-recorded [regression]: the response or report states the tone it worked to — the axis or axes it read out of 'more formal, friendly but not chatty' and where it placed the document — rather than silently absorbing the request into the rewrite.

tone-does-not-introduce-unattested-forms [regression]: formality is not borrowed from outside the profile — the rewrite contains at most 1 em dash in prose, no '--' used as a dash between words (the markdown table's delimiter row is structure and stays verbatim), no clause-joining semicolon, no sentence-initial 'However/Furthermore/Additionally/Moreover/In addition', no 'In conclusion' and no 'It's worth noting'; every one of those is an absence pattern in the profile and stays absent under a tone request.

tone-moves-inside-the-range-not-out-of-it [regression]: `textstats.py measure ORIGINAL REWRITE --db PROFILE` prints spelling-lexical/contraction with verdict `match` or `low` (inside the author's range) on the rewrite, and the rewrite's contraction count is strictly higher than the draft's 16. A formal reading may aim at the low end of the author's range; leaving contractions where the draft had them, or reducing them, means the tone left the author's voice rather than moving inside it. Reading the verdict rather than an absolute count keeps this robust to the rewrite's own length.

profile-outranks-tone-on-person [discriminating]: the formality request does not reassign who did the work — the team keeps the actions the draft credits to it, and no sentence moves an action from `we` to `I` or the reverse. Where the rewrite leaves the profile's tier-1 first-singular row below the author's range, the report names it as a deliberate call and says which sentences were ineligible, rather than reporting the row as satisfied. Silently reverting to a corporate 'we' throughout while reporting `match` is the profile being overridden rather than steered.
report-names-tone-effects [discriminating]: the report names the rows the tone moved, including any row that already matched the author and was moved for tone alone.

report-names-the-register-limit [discriminating]: the report says what the formality request could not get from this profile — that the corpus holds no formal register to aim at, so 'more formal' could only mean the formal end of the author's own measured ranges. A run that silently treats the brief as satisfiable fails: the profile's five documents are a blog post, two notes, a readme and an email, none of them formal.
structure-preserved-mechanically [discriminating]: structure_check.py on original vs. rewrite exits 0 with 0 errors.

structure-errors-not-shipped [discriminating]: no structural change is delivered with a justification attached. If structure_check.py reports an error at any point in the transcript, the run fixes the rewrite and re-runs until it exits 0; a rewrite shipped with a known error — a dissolved list explained as a profile pattern, a merged section called deliberate — fails even when the explanation is accurate about what the profile says. A profile row never licenses a structural change.
input-not-overwritten [discriminating]: evals/files/ai-draft.md is byte-identical to the fixture after the run, and the rewrite lives in a separate file next to it.

report-figures-reproduce [discriminating]: every number in the report's before/after table reproduces from `textstats.py measure ORIGINAL REWRITE --db PROFILE --db skills/write-like-me/data/ai-style-patterns.json` on the delivered file, within rounding, and so does every count the prose claims ('both semicolons', 'all five connectives', the word count). A run whose report miscounts the draft it just measured fails, however good the rewrite is: the skill's claim is machine-checked convergence, and a figure recalled from an earlier convergence round is not that.

evals.name: short-input-adds-nothing-and-reports-briefly
evals.prompt:
Quick one — I had an agent draft my reply to a PR review and it came out sounding like a press release. Can you make it sound like me? My profile is at evals/files/user-style.json. I'm on my phone, so just give me the text back. Here's the draft:

Thanks for the review! I've pushed a fix for the retry logic — it now backs off exponentially rather than hammering the endpoint. It's worth noting that the flake was not a timeout issue but a DNS one, which is why the earlier patch didn't help.
